newsitem.title: BOSNIA: U.S. soldier injured in Serb retaliatory bombing.
newsitem.headline: U.S. soldier injured in Serb retaliatory bombing.

text.p: NATO said on Saturday a U.S. soldier suffered minor injuries in a bombing attack overnight as Bosnian Serb hardliners kept up a campaign of retaliatory attacks for a Western crackdown on indicted war criminals.
NATO said the soldier was cut by flying glass after an explosive was lobbed at a car parked outside offices used by NATO military observers in the Serb-controlled town of Doboj.
It was the first injury caused by six consecutive days of small-scale explosions, although another U.S. soldier was slightly hurt when he was attacked with a sickle.
Three other bombings were reported on Friday night elsewhere in Bosnia's Serb republic, targeting a NATO base and apartments of two international police monitors.

Western officials said the low-level violence was an attempt by hardline nationalists to force the United States and European countries to drop a more aggressive stance towards suspects charged by the U.N. war crimes tribunal in The Hague.
The hardliners are loyal to former Bosnian Serb president Radovan Karadzic, who is wanted by the tribunal on charges of genocide and crimes against humanity.
The alliance-led peace force staged a modest show of force on Saturday afternoon in the mountain village of Pale which has served as headquarters for Karadzic.

Eight French armour personnel carriers joined by Italian armoured vehicles drove through Pale, outside Sarajevo, and at one point parked in front of the offices of international police -- a couple of kilometres from Karadzic's house.
The soldiers left after an hour and it was not known whether Karadzic, who is guarded by heavily-armed police, was in the house at the time.

A NATO swoop last week against two of Karadzic's allies in the northwest Prijedor region shocked the hardline leadership and fuelled speculation that the alliance might go after other fugitives, including Karadzic himself.
Karadzic once scoffed at the tribunal and international demands for his extradition but a NATO swoop last week against two of his allies shocked the hardline leadership.

British soldiers detained and extradited one suspected war criminal in Prijedor last week and shot dead another who resisted. Both were indicted for "ethnic cleansing" against Moslems and Croats early in the 1992-95 Bosnian conflict.
Western officials said the hardliners, who keep tight control over Serb territory through police and lucrative smuggling rackets, felt threatened by the NATO crackdown.
Recent bombings and other incidents appeared carefully planned to cause limited damage and generate publicity that would raise fears of NATO casualties if more arrests were carried out.
"Things in Serb territory don't happen by coincidence," said one official.
There was no sign that ordinary Serbs, preoccupied with making ends meet in a collapsing economy, were ready to take up arms against well-armed NATO troops.
The violence has been accompanied by inflammatory reports on Karadzic's television and radio network, accusing NATO of preparing to hunt down innocent Serbs.
NATO's Supreme Allied Commander, General Wesley Clark, said on Friday that retaliatory violence would not intimidate the alliance from pursuing the tougher policy towards indicted war criminals.
The swoop marked a shift in tactics for NATO which had previously ruled out arresting suspects unless peacekeeping troops happened to encounter them during their patrols.
Karadzic loyalists are also nervous about a power struggle with Bosnian Serb President Biljana Plavsic, who has turned on fellow nationalists and accused them of rampant corruption.
Plavsic told the German magazine Der Spiegel that she would not shy away from arresting Karadzic's allies if necessary.
"The constitution gives me the right to deploy the army or the police -- as a last resort," Plavsic said in an interview to be published on Monday.
Plavsic said she could not extradite Karadzic to the U.N. tribunal because it was not allowed under the Bosnian Serb constitution.
"He's also not guilty in the sense of the charges. He was a slave to his masters in Belgrade," she said.
She also alleged U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright had offered not to pursue Karadzic if he agreed to leave Bosnia for good. But Karadzic had rejected the idea.
